questions.q: Why are wetlands important, and what is the significance of the Ramsar Convention?

answer.text: Wetlands are areas where water covers the soil or lies near the surface, such as marshes, lakes, mangroves and floodplains. They are often called the kidneys of the landscape because they purify water and trap pollutants. They control floods, recharge groundwater, support a rich variety of plants and animals, and store large amounts of carbon, helping to combat climate change.

The Ramsar Convention, signed in 1971 in the Iranian city of Ramsar, is an international treaty for the conservation and wise use of wetlands. Wetlands of international importance are designated as Ramsar sites, and India has more than eighty such sites, including Chilika Lake and Keoladeo. Threatened Ramsar sites are placed on the Montreux Record.
The Convention creates a global commitment to protect these vital but fast-disappearing ecosystems.

answer: Thus wetlands are ecologically priceless, and Ramsar provides a framework to conserve them.
